content.title: What is Globalisation?

body.text: **Globalisation** is the increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies through the growth of international trade, capital flows, and the spread of technology. It is not a single event but a process accelerated by several reinforcing drivers.

**Trade liberalisation** — the removal of tariffs, quotas, and non-tariff barriers — has dramatically reduced the cost of moving goods across borders. The WTO, regional trade blocs, and bilateral agreements have all contributed. **Technology** has slashed communication and transport costs: the internet enables instant coordination across continents, while containerisation cut shipping costs by over 90% in the second half of the twentieth century.

**Capital account deregulation** allows money to flow freely between countries, enabling firms to invest abroad and savers to diversify globally. **Political changes** — the collapse of the Soviet Union, China's market reforms, and the expansion of the EU — opened up billions of new workers and consumers to the global economy.

steps: Trade barriers fall
Transport and communication costs drop
Capital flows freely across borders
Economies become deeply integrated
body.result: Globalisation — a self-reinforcing process of economic integration

sections.title: Causes of Globalisation
sections.keyIdea: Globalisation is driven by trade liberalisation, technological advances, capital deregulation, and political change — each reinforcing the others to integrate national economies.
sections.examMatters: Examiners want you to identify and explain specific causes — not just list them. Link each cause to a mechanism: trade liberalisation lowers costs, technology shrinks distance, deregulation frees capital. Always show how these causes reinforce each other.

realExample.text: China joining the WTO in 2001 is a landmark case. It committed to lowering tariffs and opening markets, which turbocharged its exports and attracted massive FDI. Within a decade China became the world's largest exporter, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.

sections.misconception: Students treat globalisation as purely about trade. Wrong — it also involves capital flows, migration, and technology transfer. Instead write: globalisation is the integration of goods, services, capital, and labour markets across national borders, driven by trade, technology, and policy changes working together.

body.text: The **benefits** of globalisation are substantial. Consumers gain access to a wider variety of goods at lower prices. Countries specialise according to comparative advantage, raising **allocative efficiency** globally. Developing nations attract FDI, which brings jobs, technology transfer, and tax revenue. The World Bank estimates that globalisation helped lift over one billion people out of extreme poverty between 1990 and 2015.

The **costs** fall unevenly. Workers in industries exposed to cheaper imports face **structural unemployment** — their skills may not transfer to growing sectors. Within-country **inequality** often rises as capital owners and skilled workers gain while low-skilled workers lose bargaining power. **Environmental damage** accelerates as production shifts to countries with weaker regulation, a process called the 'pollution haven' effect.

The net impact depends critically on domestic policy. Countries with strong education systems, safety nets, and effective regulation can capture the gains while cushioning the losers. Those without these institutions often see the costs concentrated on the most vulnerable.

sections.title: Benefits and Costs of Globalisation
sections.keyIdea: Globalisation delivers consumer gains and poverty reduction through specialisation, but creates losers through structural unemployment, rising inequality, and environmental damage.
sections.examMatters: Evaluation is everything here. A strong answer acknowledges that globalisation raises total welfare but distributes gains unevenly. Use the phrase 'it depends on' and specify: it depends on the strength of domestic institutions, the mobility of labour, and the effectiveness of redistribution policy.

realExample.text: Bangladesh's garment industry employs over four million workers, mostly women, and accounts for over 80% of export earnings. Globalisation created these jobs and raised incomes, but working conditions remain poor and wages low — illustrating both the gains and the costs.

sections.misconception: Students claim globalisation is either entirely good or entirely bad. Wrong — it creates both winners and losers simultaneously. Instead write: the net effect of globalisation depends on domestic policies — education, retraining, safety nets, and environmental regulation determine whether gains are shared or concentrated.

takeaway: Globalisation is driven by trade liberalisation, technology, capital deregulation, and political change — all reinforcing each other.
Benefits: lower prices, greater variety, poverty reduction through specialisation and FDI.
Costs: structural unemployment, rising inequality, environmental damage in weakly regulated economies.
The net impact depends on domestic policy — education, safety nets, and regulation are decisive.

content.title: Multinational Corporations

body.text: A **multinational corporation (MNC)** is a firm that produces in two or more countries. MNCs invest abroad through **foreign direct investment (FDI)** — building factories, acquiring firms, or establishing subsidiaries. The motives are clear: access to **lower labour costs**, proximity to **growing consumer markets**, and the ability to achieve greater **economies of scale** by spreading fixed costs across global output.

For the **host country**, FDI brings significant benefits. New factories create **employment**, often in regions with limited opportunities. MNCs transfer **technology and management expertise** that spills over to local firms. Tax revenue from corporate profits funds public services. Over time, the host economy may develop its own industrial capacity — a process called 'industrial upgrading'.

steps: MNC seeks lower costs or market access
FDI flows into host country
Jobs, technology, and tax revenue created
body.result: Host economy gains productive capacity and integrates into global supply chains

sections.title: Why MNCs Invest Abroad
sections.keyIdea: MNCs invest overseas to access lower costs, new markets, and economies of scale — bringing FDI that creates jobs, transfers technology, and generates tax revenue for host countries.
sections.examMatters: When evaluating FDI, distinguish between short-run and long-run effects. In the short run, jobs and tax revenue dominate. In the long run, technology transfer and supply chain development may matter more for the host country's growth trajectory.

realExample.text: Toyota opened its Burnaston factory in Derbyshire, UK, in 1992. It created over 3,000 direct jobs and thousands more in the supply chain. Local firms adopted Toyota's lean manufacturing techniques, raising productivity across the region.

sections.misconception: Students assume MNCs invest abroad only for cheap labour. Wrong — market access, avoiding trade barriers, and economies of scale are equally important motives. Instead write: MNCs choose locations based on a combination of cost, market size, infrastructure, skills, and regulatory environment.

body.text: The costs of hosting MNCs can be severe. **Profit repatriation** means that much of the value created flows back to shareholders in the home country rather than being reinvested locally. **Transfer pricing** — setting artificial prices on intra-firm transactions — allows MNCs to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, eroding the host country's tax base.

MNCs may also **exploit weak labour standards**, paying low wages and resisting unionisation. Environmental regulation in developing countries is often poorly enforced, leading to **pollution and resource depletion**. Local competitors can be crowded out if the MNC's scale advantages are insurmountable, creating **dependency** on foreign capital.

The net impact depends heavily on **host country governance**. Countries with strong institutions — transparent tax systems, enforceable labour laws, and environmental standards — capture more of the benefits. Those with weak governance may find that MNCs extract more value than they create.

sections.title: Costs of MNCs to Host Countries
sections.keyIdea: MNCs can repatriate profits, exploit transfer pricing, suppress wages, and damage the environment — the net impact on the host country depends on the strength of its governance.
sections.examMatters: Examiners reward balanced evaluation. Structure your answer: benefits (jobs, tech transfer, tax) vs costs (profit repatriation, transfer pricing, exploitation). Then evaluate: the net impact depends on the host country's institutional capacity — this is the key judgement.

realExample.text: Starbucks faced a UK public backlash in 2012 when it emerged the company had paid almost no corporation tax on billions in UK sales, using transfer pricing to shift profits to subsidiaries in the Netherlands and Switzerland.

sections.misconception: Students say MNCs are always bad for developing countries. Wrong — the evidence shows FDI is strongly associated with faster growth when governance is adequate. Instead write: MNCs bring both benefits and costs; the net effect depends on the host country's ability to regulate, tax, and channel FDI into productive uses.

takeaway: MNCs invest abroad for lower costs, market access, and economies of scale — FDI brings jobs and technology.
Costs include profit repatriation, transfer pricing, labour exploitation, and environmental damage.
The net impact on the host country depends critically on the quality of governance and regulation.

content.title: Trade Blocs

body.text: A **trade bloc** is a group of countries that agree to reduce or eliminate trade barriers between themselves. The degree of integration varies enormously, and each step involves a trade-off between the economic benefits of deeper integration and the loss of national policy autonomy.

A **free trade area (FTA)** removes tariffs between members but each country keeps its own external tariffs — like NAFTA (now USMCA). A **customs union** adds a common external tariff (CET), so all members charge the same rate on imports from outside — like the EU customs union. A **single market** goes further, allowing free movement of goods, services, capital, and labour — the EU single market is the most advanced example.

A **monetary union** adopts a single currency and central bank, eliminating exchange rate risk and transaction costs between members — like the Eurozone. Each step up the integration ladder brings greater efficiency gains but demands more coordination and less national sovereignty over trade, fiscal, and monetary policy.

sections.title: Types of Trade Bloc
sections.keyIdea: Trade blocs range from free trade areas to monetary unions — each level of integration removes more barriers but requires surrendering more national sovereignty.
sections.examMatters: Examiners expect you to sequence the types from least to most integrated (FTA, customs union, single market, monetary union) and explain what is added at each stage. Always link deeper integration to the sovereignty trade-off — more efficiency but less national policy freedom.

realExample.text: The EU single market allows 450 million people to trade, work, and invest across 27 countries without border checks. It has boosted intra-EU trade by an estimated 60%, demonstrating the power of deep integration — though it required members to accept common regulations and free movement.

sections.misconception: Students confuse free trade areas with customs unions. Wrong — the critical difference is the common external tariff. Instead write: in a free trade area each country sets its own external tariffs, but in a customs union all members apply the same tariff to non-members, which requires giving up independent trade policy.

body.text: **Trade creation** occurs when a country switches from a higher-cost domestic producer to a lower-cost member of the trade bloc. Tariffs between members fall to zero, so the cheaper partner's goods become accessible. This improves allocative efficiency — resources shift to where they are most productive.

**Trade diversion** occurs when the common external tariff (CET) forces a country to switch imports from the cheapest global supplier (outside the bloc) to a more expensive member. The tariff makes the external supplier artificially expensive, even though they are the most efficient producer. This reduces allocative efficiency.

The **net benefit** of a trade bloc depends on whether trade creation exceeds trade diversion. This is more likely when the CET is low, the bloc is large and diverse, and pre-existing tariffs were high. If the CET is set high to protect inefficient member industries, diversion dominates and the bloc makes its members worse off.

steps: Countries form customs union
Internal tariffs removed (creation)
CET applied to non-members (diversion)
body.result: Net benefit depends on whether creation outweighs diversion — lower CET makes this more likely

sections.title: Trade Creation and Trade Diversion
sections.keyIdea: Trade blocs create trade when members switch to cheaper partners inside the bloc, but divert trade when the common external tariff forces a switch away from the cheapest global supplier.
sections.examMatters: This is a favourite evaluation topic. Show trade creation and diversion on a diagram. Then evaluate: if the CET is low and the bloc covers many diverse economies, creation is likely to dominate. If the CET is high to protect specific industries, diversion may outweigh creation.

realExample.text: After Brexit, the UK lost tariff-free access to EU markets and faced new trade barriers. Some UK importers switched from EU suppliers to more expensive domestic or non-EU sources — a form of trade diversion in reverse, illustrating how leaving a bloc can redirect trade flows.

sections.misconception: Students assume trade blocs always increase trade. Wrong — while they create trade between members, they can divert trade away from more efficient non-members. Instead write: trade blocs have ambiguous welfare effects; the net impact depends on the balance between trade creation (efficiency-improving) and trade diversion (efficiency-reducing).

takeaway: Trade blocs range from FTAs (least integrated) to monetary unions (most integrated) — each step trades sovereignty for efficiency.
Trade creation shifts sourcing to cheaper bloc members; trade diversion shifts away from the cheapest global supplier.
Net benefit depends on the level of the common external tariff and the diversity of the bloc's economies.

steps: Trade barriers fall
Transport and communication costs drop
Capital flows freely across borders
flow.result: National economies become increasingly integrated and interdependent

notes.title: What is Globalisation?

items.text: Globalisation — the increasing economic integration of national economies through free trade, capital mobility, migration, and the spread of technology.
Multinational corporation (MNC) — a firm that operates in two or more countries, typically with headquarters in one country and production or sales operations abroad.
Trade liberalisation — reductions in tariffs and quotas through WTO negotiations and regional trade agreements (e.g. EU single market).
Technological advances — the internet, containerisation, and cheaper air freight have dramatically reduced the cost of moving goods, services, and information.
Capital liberalisation — deregulation of financial markets allows capital to flow freely across borders, enabling foreign direct investment (FDI).
Political changes — the collapse of the Soviet Union, China's opening up, and the expansion of the EU created new markets and production locations.

notes.keyIdea: Globalisation is the increasing integration and interdependence of national economies through trade, capital flows, migration, and technology — it is a process, not an event, and its pace has accelerated dramatically since the 1980s.
takeaway: Globalisation = economic integration through trade, capital, migration, and technology.
Key causes: trade liberalisation, technology, capital deregulation, political openness.
It is an accelerating process, not a new phenomenon.
notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to explain causes of globalisation and evaluate whether it is beneficial. Use specific examples (WTO rounds, containerisation, internet) rather than vague generalisations.
notes.misconception: Students treat globalisation as entirely new. Wrong because trade between nations has existed for centuries. Instead write: globalisation has accelerated since the 1980s due to technology and trade liberalisation, but international trade and capital flows have a long history.

steps: Markets integrate
Specialisation raises output and lowers prices
But some workers and communities lose out
flow.result: Net global benefit, but unevenly distributed — creating political backlash

notes.title: Benefits and Costs of Globalisation

items.text: Consumer benefits — greater choice, lower prices, and access to goods that could not be produced domestically.
Efficiency gains — international specialisation according to comparative advantage raises global output.
Economic growth — FDI transfers capital, technology, and management skills to developing economies, raising productivity.
Poverty reduction — export-led growth in countries like China and India has lifted hundreds of millions out of absolute poverty.
Structural unemployment — workers in industries that cannot compete with cheap imports lose jobs and may lack the skills for new sectors.
Widening inequality — skilled workers and capital owners gain more than unskilled workers, widening the income distribution within countries.
Environmental damage — increased production and transport raise carbon emissions; some firms relocate to countries with weaker environmental regulations.
Evaluation: globalisation raises average welfare but does not raise everyone's welfare — the distribution of gains matters as much as the total size.

notes.keyIdea: Globalisation creates winners and losers — it raises average incomes through specialisation and competition, but can widen inequality within countries and leave some workers and communities behind.
takeaway: Benefits: lower prices, greater choice, FDI, poverty reduction through export-led growth.
Costs: structural unemployment, inequality, environmental damage, loss of sovereignty.
Net positive on average, but distribution of gains is highly uneven.
notes.examMatters: Examiners want balanced evaluation. Acknowledge that globalisation raises total welfare through specialisation, but emphasise that the gains are unevenly distributed. Use specific examples and always consider short-run vs long-run effects.
notes.misconception: Students say globalisation is either all good or all bad. Wrong because it creates winners and losers simultaneously. Instead write: globalisation increases total output through specialisation and competition, but the gains accrue disproportionately to skilled workers and capital owners, while low-skilled workers in developed countries may lose out.

steps: MNC invests in host country (FDI)
Jobs, technology, and exports increase
But profits repatriated, tax minimised
flow.result: Net impact depends on the balance between investment benefits and profit extraction

notes.title: Multinational Corporations (MNCs)

items.text: Lower costs — cheaper labour, land, and raw materials in developing countries reduce production costs.
Market access — producing locally avoids trade barriers and allows the firm to respond to local consumer preferences.
Economies of scale — spreading production across multiple countries allows the firm to operate at a larger, more efficient scale.
Positive: FDI creates jobs, transfers technology and skills, generates tax revenue, and boosts exports.
Negative: profits are repatriated, local firms are crowded out, working conditions may be poor, and MNCs can use transfer pricing to minimise tax.
Transfer pricing — MNCs shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions by manipulating the prices charged between subsidiaries, reducing tax paid in the host country.
MNCs link to the balance of payments (4.3.3): FDI inflows improve the capital account but profit repatriation worsens the current account.

notes.keyIdea: MNCs are the primary vehicle of globalisation — they bring investment, jobs, and technology to host countries, but their market power raises concerns about exploitation, tax avoidance, and political influence.
takeaway: MNCs invest abroad for: lower costs, market access, economies of scale.
Benefits: jobs, technology transfer, tax revenue. Costs: profit repatriation, transfer pricing.
Net impact depends on host-country governance and regulatory strength.
notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to evaluate MNCs using specific arguments: FDI, technology transfer, and job creation vs profit repatriation, transfer pricing, and crowding out of local firms. Always consider whether the host government can effectively regulate MNC behaviour.
notes.misconception: Students say MNCs always exploit developing countries. Wrong because FDI often raises wages above the local average, transfers technology, and creates export opportunities. Instead write: MNCs bring significant benefits to host countries, but the distribution of gains depends on the bargaining power of the host government and the regulatory framework.

steps: Countries form trade bloc
Internal barriers removed → trade creation
External barriers may cause trade diversion
flow.result: Net benefit depends on whether trade creation outweighs trade diversion

notes.title: Trade Blocs

items.text: Free trade area (FTA) — member countries remove tariffs between each other but keep their own external tariffs against non-members (e.g. USMCA/NAFTA).
Customs union — members remove internal tariffs and adopt a common external tariff (CET) against non-members (e.g. EU customs union).
Single/common market — a customs union plus free movement of labour, capital, and services (e.g. EU single market).
Monetary union — members share a common currency and central bank (e.g. eurozone).
Trade creation — a trade bloc allows consumers to switch from high-cost domestic producers to lower-cost member producers, increasing welfare.
Trade diversion — the CET causes consumers to switch from low-cost non-member producers to higher-cost member producers, reducing welfare.
A trade bloc increases welfare if trade creation > trade diversion. Whether this holds depends on the CET level and how competitive member producers are.
Trade blocs link to comparative advantage (4.3.2): they promote specialisation among members but may prevent specialisation with the rest of the world.

notes.keyIdea: Trade blocs remove barriers between members but may create them against non-members — the key question is whether they promote free trade globally or fragment the world into competing trading clubs.
takeaway: FTA → customs union → single market → monetary union (increasing integration).
Trade creation = good (switch to cheaper member producer).
Trade diversion = bad (switch away from cheapest global producer due to CET).
notes.examMatters: Examiners expect you to use the trade creation vs trade diversion framework. Always define both terms, draw a diagram if possible, and conclude with 'it depends on' the level of the CET and the competitiveness of member producers.
notes.misconception: Students assume trade blocs always promote free trade. Wrong because while they remove barriers between members, the common external tariff may raise barriers against non-members. Instead write: trade blocs promote regional free trade but may divert trade away from more efficient non-member producers.

diagrams.title: Costs vs Benefits of Globalisation
checklist: List all key benefits on one side: growth, tax revenue, EoS, lower prices, consumer surplus, choice, living standards
List all key costs on the other side: structural unemployment, exploitation, environment, transfer pricing, inequality, TNC influence
Highlight the distributional dimension: benefits are diffuse (spread widely) while costs are concentrated (specific groups/regions)
Note the evaluation point: the net effect depends on context, policy, and who is affected
Reference specific groups who gain (consumers, TNCs, skilled workers) and who lose (low-skilled workers, some developing countries)
diagrams.description: A balance diagram comparing the main benefits and costs of globalisation, highlighting the distributional dimension of who gains and who loses.

flashcards.back: The increasing interdependence and integration of the world's economies through cross-border trade, investment, migration, and the spread of technology.
Trade liberalisation (WTO, reduced tariffs), technological advances (internet, containerisation), deregulation of financial markets, and the growth of multinational corporations.
A firm that operates in more than one country, with production or service facilities outside its home country. E.g., Apple, Toyota, Unilever.
FDI inflows (jobs, capital, technology transfer), access to larger export markets, and higher economic growth rates from integration into global supply chains.
flashcards.front: Name three benefits of globalisation for developing countries.

flashcards.back: Deindustrialisation in developed countries, exploitation of cheap labour in developing countries, and environmental degradation from increased production and transport.
Investment by a firm in productive capacity in another country — e.g., building a factory abroad. Brings capital, jobs, and technology transfer to the host country.
The decline of manufacturing as a share of GDP and employment. Often caused by globalisation as production moves to lower-cost countries.
A group of countries that agree to reduce or eliminate trade barriers between members — e.g., EU, ASEAN, NAFTA/USMCA. Promotes trade within the bloc but may divert trade from non-members.
The World Trade Organisation — promotes free trade by negotiating trade agreements, resolving disputes, and reducing tariffs. 164 member countries.
The use of standardised shipping containers to transport goods. Dramatically reduced transport costs and time, making global trade cheaper and faster.
When MNCs set internal prices for transactions between subsidiaries in different countries to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions. Reduces tax payments but is controversial.
The emigration of skilled workers from developing to developed countries. Benefits the destination country but reduces human capital in the origin country.
The spread of dominant cultures (often Western) at the expense of local traditions — through global brands, media, and consumer habits. A criticism of globalisation.
The removal or reduction of trade barriers (tariffs, quotas, regulations) to encourage free movement of goods and services between countries.
The internet enables instant communication and e-commerce, cheaper air travel increases mobility, and automation reduces production costs — all making cross-border activity easier.
MNCs create direct jobs in their operations and indirect jobs through supply chains. However, they may also crowd out local firms and exploit low wages.
flashcards.front: What is the impact of MNCs on host country employment?

flashcards.back: Relocating business processes to another country — usually to reduce costs. Can involve the firm's own subsidiary (FDI) or outsourcing to a foreign company.
Contracting a business function to a third party rather than performing it in-house. Reduces costs but may reduce quality and control.

options: A decrease in the proportion of trade relative to GDP
An increase in trade as a proportion of GDP and a rise in FDI flows
A decrease in the number of transnational corporations operating worldwide
Reduced international migration and lower remittance flows
quiz.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic of globalisation?
quiz.explanation: Globalisation is characterised by an increase in trade as a proportion of GDP, a rise in FDI flows and TNC activity, and an increase in international migration. All three indicators have shown upward trends since the 1980s. Options A, C, and D describe the opposite of what has occurred during globalisation.

options: Imposing tariffs on member countries to protect domestic industries
Facilitating the reduction of trade barriers through multilateral negotiations
Encouraging countries to adopt protectionist trade policies
Establishing a single global currency for international trade
quiz.question: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has contributed to globalisation primarily by:
quiz.explanation: The WTO (successor to GATT) has promoted globalisation by facilitating multilateral trade liberalisation, reducing average tariffs from over 40% to under 5%, enforcing trade rules including the Most Favoured Nation principle, and providing a dispute settlement mechanism. The WTO promotes free trade, not protectionism (Options A and C). It has no role in currency (Option D).

options: The formation of the European Economic Community in 1957
The adoption of the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system
The collapse of the Soviet Union bringing former communist states into the global market economy
The introduction of the gold standard in major economies
quiz.question: Which political change was a significant cause of the acceleration of globalisation in the 1990s?
quiz.explanation: The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 was a key political cause of accelerated globalisation, bringing approximately 400 million people in former communist states into the global market economy, opening new markets for trade and investment. The EEC (A) was formed much earlier. Bretton Woods (B) collapsed in 1971. The gold standard (D) pre-dates modern globalisation.

options: Increase tariff barriers against imports from that country
Access lower labour costs and enter new consumer markets
Reduce the volume of international trade
Increase the exchange rate of the home country's currency
quiz.question: A transnational corporation (TNC) is most likely to undertake foreign direct investment (FDI) in a developing country in order to:
quiz.explanation: TNCs undertake FDI in developing countries primarily to access lower labour costs (reducing production costs) and to enter new, growing consumer markets. Other motives include accessing natural resources, exploiting economies of scale, and benefiting from favourable tax regimes. FDI has nothing to do with raising tariffs (A), reducing trade (C), or directly affecting exchange rates (D).

options: Increased profit repatriation to the TNC's home country
Technology transfer and knowledge spillovers to domestic firms
A 'race to the bottom' on labour and environmental standards
Greater dependency on volatile foreign capital inflows
quiz.question: Which of the following is a positive impact of FDI on a recipient developing country?
quiz.explanation: Technology transfer is a key positive impact of FDI: TNCs bring advanced technologies, production techniques, and management practices that can spill over to domestic firms, boosting productivity and economic development. Options A, C, and D are all negative impacts or concerns associated with FDI, not benefits.

options: Increases the wages paid to local workers
Encourages more greenfield investment in the host country
Allows TNCs to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, reducing tax revenue
Leads to higher import tariffs being imposed by the host country
quiz.question: Transfer pricing by TNCs is a concern for host country governments because it:
quiz.explanation: Transfer pricing involves TNCs manipulating prices between their own subsidiaries across countries to shift profits to low-tax jurisdictions, thereby reducing the tax revenue collected by host country governments. Estimates suggest developing countries lose over $100 billion annually. It does not increase wages (A), encourage investment (B), or relate to tariffs (D).

options: Higher prices for imported goods due to increased transportation costs
Reduced variety of products available in domestic markets
Lower prices and greater choice as imports from lower-cost producers increase competition
Guaranteed employment security in domestic manufacturing industries
quiz.question: One benefit of globalisation for consumers in developed countries is:
quiz.explanation: Globalisation benefits consumers through lower prices (due to cheaper imports, increased competition, and economies of scale) and greater choice of products from around the world. This increases consumer surplus and real purchasing power. Transport costs have actually fallen (A is wrong). Variety has increased, not decreased (B). Globalisation can actually threaten some manufacturing jobs (D).

options: All workers receive equally higher wages from increased trade
Skilled workers benefit from higher demand while low-skilled workers face wage pressure from foreign competition
Governments always redistribute the gains from trade equally
TNCs are required to pay the same wages in every country they operate
quiz.question: Globalisation is most likely to increase income inequality within developed countries because:
quiz.explanation: Globalisation tends to widen inequality within developed countries because highly skilled workers benefit from increased demand and higher returns, while low-skilled workers face wage stagnation or decline due to competition from cheaper labour in developing countries and the offshoring of routine tasks. The gains are not equally shared (A), governments do not always redistribute effectively (C), and TNCs exploit international wage differences rather than equalising them (D).

options: Countries competing to have the highest environmental and labour standards to attract FDI
Countries lowering tax rates, labour protections, and environmental standards to compete for TNC investment
The tendency for exchange rates to depreciate uniformly across all countries
The reduction in tariff rates through WTO negotiations
quiz.question: The concept of a 'race to the bottom' in the context of globalisation refers to:
quiz.explanation: A 'race to the bottom' occurs when countries competitively lower taxes, weaken labour protections, and relax environmental regulations to attract FDI from TNCs. This can undermine worker welfare, environmental protection, and government revenues. Option A describes the opposite. Option C is unrelated. Option D describes trade liberalisation, which is a separate process from the competitive lowering of standards.

options: Globalisation is entirely beneficial because it always increases GDP for every country
Globalisation is entirely harmful because it only benefits TNCs at the expense of workers
The net impact of globalisation depends on country-specific factors such as institutional quality, government policy, and how gains are distributed
Globalisation has no significant effect on either economic growth or inequality
quiz.question: Which of the following is the most valid evaluative point about the overall impact of globalisation?
quiz.explanation: The most balanced and valid evaluative point is that globalisation's net impact depends on context: the quality of a country's institutions, the effectiveness of government policies in managing adjustment costs and distributing gains, the type of integration (FDI, trade, migration), and the specific sectors affected. Both extreme positions (entirely beneficial or entirely harmful) are oversimplified. Evidence clearly shows globalisation has significant effects (ruling out D).

common_mistakes.title: Treating globalisation as purely economic
common_mistakes.mistake: Students only discuss trade and FDI without mentioning political, social, and technological dimensions.
common_mistakes.correction: Globalisation has economic (trade, FDI), political (trade liberalisation, WTO), technological (internet, transport), and social (migration, cultural exchange) dimensions. A complete answer covers multiple dimensions.

common_mistakes.title: Not distinguishing between different types of FDI
common_mistakes.mistake: Students discuss FDI generically without considering whether it is greenfield investment or mergers/acquisitions.
common_mistakes.correction: Greenfield FDI (building new facilities) tends to create more jobs and technology transfer. M&A FDI (buying existing firms) may lead to rationalisation and job cuts. The type of FDI matters for evaluating impact.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming globalisation benefits all countries equally
common_mistakes.mistake: Students say globalisation increases growth without noting the uneven distribution of gains.
common_mistakes.correction: Globalisation tends to benefit countries with strong institutions, skilled labour, and good infrastructure more. LDCs may be exploited through unfair terms of trade, environmental degradation, and loss of tax revenue.

practice.guidance: Globalisation is the increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies (1 mark) through the growth of international trade, capital flows, migration and the spread of technology (1 mark). It has been facilitated by reductions in trade barriers, advances in communications and transport technology, and the activities of transnational corporations (1 mark). As a result, goods, services, capital and labour move more freely across national borders (1 mark).
practice.question: Define the term 'globalisation'. (4 marks)

practice.guidance:
Way 1: Foreign direct investment (FDI) (1 mark) — TNCs invest in production facilities, distribution networks and subsidiaries in multiple countries, creating cross-border supply chains that integrate economies (1 mark). For example, Apple designs in the US, sources components from Asia and assembles in China (1 mark).

Way 2: Technology and knowledge transfer (1 mark) — TNCs bring advanced production methods, management techniques and technology to host countries, raising productivity and spreading innovation globally (1 mark). This accelerates economic integration as developing countries adopt practices from more advanced economies (1 mark).
practice.question: Explain two ways in which transnational corporations (TNCs) contribute to globalisation. (6 marks)

practice.guidance: Define FDI as investment by a firm in one country into business operations in another country, typically involving ownership or control of productive assets (2 marks). Benefits: creates employment and raises incomes in the host country (2 marks); brings technology transfer, new skills and managerial expertise that can raise productivity (2 marks). Costs: profits may be repatriated to the TNC's home country rather than reinvested locally, causing a leakage from the circular flow (2 marks); TNCs may exploit lax environmental or labour regulations, and use transfer pricing to minimise tax payments in the host country (1 mark). Judgement: the net impact depends on the regulatory framework and bargaining power of the host government — FDI is most beneficial when accompanied by strong governance (1 mark).
practice.question: Assess the impact of foreign direct investment (FDI) on developing countries. (10 marks)

practice.guidance:
Introduction: Define globalisation as the increasing integration of world economies through trade, capital flows and migration (2 marks).

For — benefits: Access to larger export markets has driven rapid economic growth in countries such as China and Vietnam, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty (3 marks); FDI brings capital, technology and employment that developing countries lack domestically (2 marks); consumers benefit from a wider variety of cheaper goods through increased trade (2 marks).

Against — harmful effects: Increased competition from imports can destroy infant industries before they become internationally competitive (3 marks); TNCs may exploit cheap labour and weak environmental regulations, creating a 'race to the bottom' (2 marks); globalisation can increase inequality within developing countries as skilled and urban workers gain more than unskilled and rural workers (2 marks).

Evaluation: The net impact depends on the country's institutions, governance and policies (2 marks). Countries with strong education systems, stable governance and strategic trade policies — such as South Korea — have benefited greatly, while those lacking these conditions have seen fewer gains or been left behind. Globalisation is not inherently beneficial or harmful; the outcome depends on how well countries manage the process (2 marks).
practice.question: Evaluate the view that globalisation has been more beneficial than harmful for developing countries. (20 marks)

practice.guidance:
Reason 1: Tax minimisation — TNCs can set artificially high or low prices on intra-firm transactions to shift profits to subsidiaries located in countries with lower corporate tax rates (1 mark), reducing their overall global tax liability (1 mark).

Reason 2: Avoidance of tariffs or exchange controls — by manipulating the prices of goods traded between subsidiaries, TNCs can reduce the value of imports into countries with high tariff barriers (1 mark), or move profits out of countries with strict capital controls (1 mark).
practice.question: Outline two reasons why TNCs may use transfer pricing. (4 marks)

steps: Reductions in tariffs, quotas and other trade barriers — driven by WTO negotiations and bilateral trade agreements — have lowered the cost of international trade.
Lower trade costs enable firms to access larger global markets, exploiting economies of scale and specialising according to comparative advantage.
Increased trade boosts economic growth in participating countries through higher exports, greater foreign direct investment and technology transfer.
Consumers benefit from lower prices, greater product variety and access to goods that cannot be produced domestically, increasing consumer welfare.
chains.title: Trade liberalisation drives globalisation and growth
chains.result: Trade liberalisation has been the primary driver of globalisation, generating growth and consumer welfare gains through specialisation and market expansion.

steps: Transnational corporations (TNCs) invest in developing countries through foreign direct investment (FDI), establishing production facilities to exploit lower labour costs and access new markets.
FDI brings benefits including job creation, technology transfer, management expertise and tax revenue that can fund public services and infrastructure.
However, TNCs may exploit weak labour and environmental regulations in developing countries, paying low wages, creating poor working conditions and causing environmental degradation.
Profits are often repatriated to the home country rather than reinvested locally, and transfer pricing strategies can reduce tax payments to host governments.
chains.title: TNCs bring FDI but can exploit developing countries
chains.result: TNCs and FDI create a complex mix of benefits and costs for developing countries — the net impact depends on host country governance and bargaining power.

steps: Globalisation creates winners and losers — skilled workers and capital owners benefit from access to global markets, while low-skilled workers face competition from cheaper labour abroad.
Offshoring and automation, both accelerated by globalisation, reduce demand for low-skilled manufacturing jobs in developed countries, depressing wages at the bottom of the distribution.
At the same time, globalisation increases returns to capital, entrepreneurship and high skills, as these factors can exploit global markets — widening income inequality.
Rising within-country inequality can erode social cohesion, fuel populist political movements and undermine support for further trade liberalisation.
chains.title: Globalisation increases inequality within countries
chains.result: Globalisation tends to increase inequality within countries by rewarding mobile factors (capital, skills) while displacing immobile low-skilled workers.

steps: Advances in information and communication technology (ICT) have dramatically reduced the costs of communication, coordination and information sharing across borders.
Containerisation and improvements in transport infrastructure have lowered shipping costs, making it economical to fragment production across multiple countries in global supply chains.
Digital platforms enable even small firms and individuals to participate in global trade, reducing the importance of physical proximity and traditional barriers to entry.
These technological changes have made globalisation self-reinforcing — lower costs encourage more integration, which drives further innovation in logistics and communication.
chains.title: Technology reduces costs and accelerates integration
chains.result: Technological progress in communication and transport has been a fundamental enabler of globalisation, reducing costs and accelerating economic integration.

evaluation.title: Globalisation's benefits are unevenly distributed
evaluation.content: While globalisation has raised aggregate global welfare and lifted millions out of absolute poverty, its benefits have been concentrated among skilled workers, capital owners and consumers in developed countries. The costs — job displacement, wage stagnation and environmental degradation — fall disproportionately on vulnerable groups. Effective redistribution policies are needed to ensure the gains from globalisation are shared more equitably.

evaluation.title: Dependency on global supply chains creates vulnerability
evaluation.content: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of globally integrated supply chains. Just-in-time production and geographic concentration of key inputs (semiconductors in East Asia, PPE in China) left countries vulnerable to disruption. This has prompted a reassessment of globalisation, with some governments pursuing reshoring and 'friend-shoring' strategies, accepting higher costs for greater supply chain resilience.

evaluation.title: The race to the bottom may be overstated
evaluation.content: Critics argue that globalisation forces countries to compete by lowering labour, environmental and tax standards — a 'race to the bottom'. However, evidence suggests that FDI often flows to countries with stronger institutions and higher standards, as these provide greater certainty and productivity. Countries that attract FDI through deregulation may find it unsustainable as social and environmental costs mount.
